In SCOPe 2.08, d1a14h2 (sunid 343393; residues H:1-8) is not a protein domain. It is an expression/purification tag, which SCOPe files under the Artifacts class: l (Artifacts) > l.1 Tags fold > l.1.1 Tags superfamily > l.1.1.1 Tags family > protein 'N-terminal Tags' (sunid 310894) > species 'Synthetic' (sunid 311501). So it is a synthetic N-terminal extension added during construction. It is not part of the natural immunoglobulin sequence. The SCOPe sequence endpoint returned no public sequence for d1a14h2, so I did not check its residue identities.

The real biological domain in the chain is d1a14h1 (sunid 20061; residues H:9-111). It is classified as b.1.1.1: class b (all beta) > fold b.1 (immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich) > superfamily b.1.1 (Immunoglobulin) > family b.1.1.1 (V set domains) > protein 'Immunoglobulin heavy chain variable domain, VH' > species 'Mouse (Mus musculus), cluster 3.2'. The SCOPe comment says it is part of Fab NC10, with only Fv coordinates included.

The l-class 'fold', 'superfamily' and 'family' levels are bookkeeping containers. They do not imply shared structure or common evolutionary origin. Two proteins that both carry similar tags share an engineering choice, not ancestry.

So similarity to d1a14h2, or to any l.1.1.1 tag, should not be treated as evidence of protein homology. Before inferring homology from a sequence or structure hit, mask or remove the tag. Do not move the tag's l.1 label onto the antibody, and do not move the VH classification onto the tag. Any homology claim for 1a14 chain H must rest on the VH region (residues 9-111) and its b.1.1.1 assignment. Even there, a shared b.1 fold by itself is weaker than shared superfamily or family membership. The N-terminal tag says nothing about function and is not useful as a template for modelling.
